note: Plain-English definitions adapted from dev-team/research/industry-tools-and-plain-english-2026-10-30.md (section 3A) and this project's docs/METRICS.md. Source tags: 'checked' = source opened by the research seat on 2026-10-30; 'reference' = canonical reference named but not re-opened; 'project' = this project's own definition; 'unverified' = plain-English wording with no external source yet.

terms.def: An S-shaped line fitted through the standards. It turns the color reading of a well into an amount of antibody. Its four numbers set the bottom, the top, the middle point and the steepness.

terms.full: Attributable, Legible, Contemporaneous, Original, Accurate, plus Complete, Consistent, Enduring, Available
terms.def: A checklist for trustworthy records: who did it, can you read it, was it written at the time, is it the original, is it correct, and is nothing missing.
Any lab test that measures how much of something is in a sample.
The unit for antibody amount in this assay. 'Arbitrary' means it is set by the test's own reference standard, not a physical weight, so it only compares results from the same test.
An automatic, permanent log of who changed a record, when, what changed and why.
A well with no sample in it. It shows the background color of the plate, which is subtracted from every other reading.
The unbroken record of every hand a sample passed through: collected, received, aliquoted, assayed, stored. A missing step is a gap.
A likely range for the true value. A wider range means we are less sure. Here it is written as 'likely range'.
A cautious way to put a likely range around a percentage, which still works when the answer is 0% or 100%.
A sample with a known amount that runs on every plate. If the plate reads it wrong, the whole plate is not trusted.
How far two repeat readings of the same sample disagree, as a percent of their average. Here, more than 20% between the duplicate wells is a fail.
Open-source software that builds report tables from SQL and runs automatic data tests on them.
A lab test that uses a color change to measure how much of a specific antibody is in a sample. More antibody gives more color.
Rules for labs that test samples from human trials, so the results can be trusted.
On average, how many times a person's antibody level went up from Day 1. Only people with both a Day 1 and a later result count.
The typical antibody level of a group. It is an average that suits numbers growing by multiples, so one very high person cannot drag it up.
The family of 'good practice' rules (lab, clinical, manufacturing) that make sure medicines are safe and records are trustworthy.
A 64-character fingerprint of a record. Change one letter and the fingerprint changes completely. Each audit row also includes the previous row's hash, so the rows form a chain.
How strongly a vaccine makes the body produce an immune response, such as antibodies.
Software that tracks every sample, test and result in a lab. Here a small one ('mini-LIMS') is built in DuckDB.
terms.src: ASTM E1578, Standard Guide for Laboratory Informatics

terms.def: The smallest amount the test can measure reliably. Below it, we write '<LLOQ' instead of guessing a number.
How much light the colored liquid in a well blocks. The plate reader measures it. Darker color gives a higher OD.

terms.full: U.S. Code of Federal Regulations, Title 21, Part 11
terms.def: The U.S. rule for when electronic records and e-signatures can be trusted like paper and ink.
A dummy shot with no vaccine in it. Comparing against it shows what the vaccine itself did.
A plastic tray with 96 small wells in 8 rows (A to H) and 12 columns. One plate holds standards, controls, blanks and samples.
Automatic checks that decide whether a plate or a result can be trusted. Each check has a rule code, such as CTRL_OOR.
Testing a sample again, for example on a new plate or at a stronger dilution, because the first result could not be used.
A person counts as 'responded' if their antibody level rose at least 4 times from Day 1. If Day 1 was too low to measure, the later value must reach 4 times the LLOQ (182.88 AU/mL).
Written step-by-step instructions everyone must follow for a task.
A reference line made from wells with known amounts. We read unknown samples off it.
Made-up data from a seeded computer generator. No real person, trial, lab or company is described.
How much antibody a sample holds. Higher means more antibody.
The largest amount the test can measure reliably. Above it, we write '>ULOQ' and test again at a stronger dilution.
